body_markdown:
On November 23, after a short period of speculation, CrowdStrike[confirmed its intention](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/press-releases/crowdstrike-to-acquire-zscaler-bringing-network-security-and-zero-trust-to-the-falcon-platform/) to acquire Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at $43.9B, making it the largest cybersecurity acquisition ever. Unsurprisingly, the primary motivation appears to be growth as CrowdStrike adds network and secure access service edge (SASE) to its broad and growing platform. The acquisition gives CrowdStrike access to Zscaler’s 11,000 customers (with 8,000 of these non-overlapping). The company estimates that the additional capabilities will increase its total addressable market (TAM) by $185B, especially as the combined organization increases its focus on AI security.


In an email, CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz stated:


*We’ve partnered with Zscaler for years, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 integrations. Many of you have long asked us to join forces and today, we’re taking that step forward. After closing, that means one platform, one data layer, and one contract. You’ll be able to add Zscaler on Falcon Flex.*


This fits the trajectory of previous mega-mergers — such as[Cisco and Splunk](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/splunk-is-good-for-cisco-but-cisco-needs-to-convince-splunk-customers-that-cisco-is-good-for-them/) ,[Palo Alto Networks and CyberArk](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/palo-alto-networks-enters-the-identity-security-market-with-25b-purchase-of-cyberark/) , or[Proofpoint and Varonis](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/proofpoint-varonis-the-platform-promise-meets-the-integration-test/?ref_search=3208447_1795489890446) — but it’s uncharacteristically large for CrowdStrike. Its acquisitions have tended to be tuck-in deals — the last three of which (SGNL, Seraphic, and Dreadnode) totaled a modest $1.2B — to expand into adjacent markets and/or acquire IP.


On a lighter note, both companies sponsor competing F1 teams (Mercedes-AMG Petronas for CrowdStrike and Aston Martin Aramco for Zscaler). Now, they’re going from sharing the F1 grid to sharing a balance sheet. That’s certainly one way to consolidate your pit crew.


## Securing AI Continues To Be The Said Reason For The Season


Securing agentic AI and delivering “Zero Trust for AI safety” are additional stated key drivers for the acquisition. The acquisition positions CrowdStrike to sit in the path of agents running on endpoints and interacting with cloud applications. Both companies have invested heavily in solutions to secure AI. The acquisition doubles down on that strategy.


The acquisition also seems to signal a CrowdStrike strategy change from smaller, focused acquisitions — and other large vendors’ AI security acquisitions mostly favoring early-stage startups — to one that mirrors other platform providers’ acquisitions of bigger, broader, and, in some cases, overlapping capabilities. For example, SGNL and Seraphic provided capabilities that were both new to CrowdStrike and complementary to each other in important ways. Those capabilities also filled specific but important gaps in existing platforms, which enabled CrowdStrike to deliver value without protracted competitive battles to displace existing technology.


## Getting The Deal Across The Finish Line


Both companies will remain separate until the deal closes during the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal year 2028 (calendar 2027). As with all acquisitions, there’s some uncertainty about the future. Short- and long-term obstacles must be overcome before the deal can be considered a success. Those include:


- **Shareholder approval won’t be a hurdle; regulatory clearance might be.** Jay Chaudhry and his affiliates control about 34% of Zscaler’s shares and have committed to support the deal. The regulatory environment in the US is favorable but is less so in the EU and UK. Direct product overlap between endpoint security and SSE is limited, but regulators could examine whether CrowdStrike might use Falcon Flex to favor Zscaler or make it harder for customers to integrate competing endpoint detection and response (EDR) platforms, such as Microsoft Defender or SentinelOne. Any concerns are more likely to result in interoperability commitments than an outright block. European investment screening could also add filings and extend the timetable. CrowdStrike’s expected H2 2027 close already leaves considerable room for regulatory review.
- **Digesting an acquisition this big makes a Thanksgiving feast small potatoes.** Despite a solid track record, CrowdStrike has never integrated something this big. Its past acquisitions were relatively small companies that added specific capabilities to the existing platform. Zscaler has thousands of customers, its own channel, and its own cloud with 200 service locations that handle 750 billion transactions a day. The $500M in promised cost synergies is expected to come mainly from data centers; however, merging that infrastructure means touching the infrastructure that delivers the performance Zscaler customers depend on. In light of the recent spate of high-profile outages across government and the tech sector, CrowdStrike will have to manage customer perceptions just as carefully as it manages the underlying transition.


## The Platform Promise Is Coming Home


CrowdStrike and Zscaler already share more than 2,000 customers and have 16 integrations, so the acquisition alone won’t transform the technical experience for customers overnight. Much of the immediate value is commercial, including bringing Zscaler products into Falcon Flex and expanding reach through each vendor’s partner ecosystem. The combination promises to “unite endpoint security with Zero Trust SASE to deliver a unified platform that puts both controls in the adversary’s path to stop breaches.” As more details emerge, customers should:


- **Look past promises of faster AI-driven integration.** This is just the latest move in a long push toward platforms that, like any major trend, has[benefits and drawbacks](https://www.forrester.com/report/understand-the-benefits-and-drawbacks-of-cybersecuritys-platform-push/RES184361) . Don’t consolidate based solely on a “one platform” promise. Require demonstrated interoperability, effective policy enforcement, and measurable operational benefits. CISOs must watch what actually changes: whether telemetry, policies, and workflows become meaningfully more integrated and whether CrowdStrike takes complexity away from security teams instead of simply putting more products on the same contract. Having a single contract, agent, or console isn’t, by itself, proof of integration.
- **Use renewal discussions to hedge against future changes.** This deal creates an opportunity to seek price protection, continuity of support for third-party integrations, and clear termination and data-export rights if material changes undermine the service. Any change-of-control protections should explicitly address the announced transaction.
- **Ask what vendor neutrality means for Red Canary after the acquisition.** Red Canary built its managed detection and response (MDR) business around supporting customers across endpoint platforms, including CrowdStrike, Microsoft, and SentinelOne. That model becomes more complicated when its ultimate owner also owns Falcon. Customers using Red Canary with competing EDR and extended detection and response (XDR) platforms should ask whether those integrations will receive the same investment, how detection engineering will work across non-Falcon telemetry, and who owns response when an incident crosses technology boundaries. Those questions matter most during the handoff from[MDR to incident response](https://www.forrester.com/report/best-practices-for-mdr-to-ir-handoffs/RES192720?ref_search=604835_1795443956081) , where unclear ownership can delay critical decisions.
- **Assess how platform consolidation impacts operational risk.** The combined company would deliver an endpoint agent that’s deployed deep into customer environments and a Zero Trust access path that many customers rely on to reach applications and services. Although the underlying infrastructure will likely remain separate in the near term, consolidation seems inevitable. The[July 2024 CrowdStrike outage](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/crowdstrike-global-outage-critical-next-steps-for-tech-and-security-leaders/?ref_search=604835_1795444178832) showed how quickly a failure in a widely deployed security control becomes a business disruption. CISOs considering broader consolidation onto the combined platform should evaluate the dependency it creates and ensure degraded-mode access, out-of-band communications, and recovery capabilities don’t depend on the same technology they’re trying to recover from.


## Mind The Gaps, Manage The Overlaps


Like many platform vendor acquisitions, this pairing comes with its share of overlapping capabilities. At the same time, capability gaps remain. Inevitably, some capabilities will flourish while others may wither or be cut entirely. While evaluating and tracking the evolution of the combined offerings, remember:


- **Choose your future cloud security solution wisely — it exists in both platforms.** With its native cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP) and its acquired SaaS security posture management (SSPM) capabilities, CrowdStrike is a formidable player. Zscaler dabbled in CNAPP but apparently exited the market around 2024 — though the IP is presumably still in a drawer. Zscaler also offers an[SSPM](https://www.zscaler.com/products-and-solutions/saas-security) solution that clearly overlaps with CrowdStrike’s[Falcon Shield](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/platform/falcon-shield/) . Enterprises should ask the combined vendor about roadmaps to inform their future cloud security investments.
- **Seriously consider CrowdStrike for data security, it will be differentiated.** CrowdStrike customers that hesitated to adopt Falcon Data Security — while waiting for it to reach greater parity with alternatives — now have a reason to more seriously consider data security controls like data loss prevention and masking via Zscaler. Differentiation outcomes — beyond what each provider offers separately today — depend on meaningful integration to reconcile the underlying data security posture management foundations of both platforms, as well as existing strengths from CrowdStrike, such as endpoint telemetry to inform data risks and controls.
- **Monitor email security partnerships — basic social engineering attacks remain.** While effective, endpoint security and Zero Trust still don’t cover the entire attack surface. Most effective attacks don’t need to exploit an endpoint or bypass a network control — instead, they use phishing and social engineering techniques. Attackers can move from phishing into collaboration channels, impersonate the help desk, and convince an employee to use legitimate remote-access tools or hand over credentials. CrowdStrike relies on[email security partners](https://www.forrester.com/report/the-email-messaging-and-collaboration-security-solutions-landscape-q4-2026/RES200000216) like[Proofpoint](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/proofpoint-varonis-the-platform-promise-meets-the-integration-test/) and Abnormal AI to cover email and collaboration platforms. Acquiring Zscaler doesn’t change that. Email security buyers should watch what happens to those partnerships as CrowdStrike expands its platform ambitions.
- **Evaluate identity solutions based on your use case(s).** Despite CrowdStrike having announced Agentic Identity Provider (Agentic IdP) earlier this year, neither it nor Zscaler have a true IdP and identity access management (IAM) solution that covers business user and privileged user governance, provisioning, access reviews, and access policy enforcement. CrowdStrike’s identity threat detection and response capabilities are necessary but not sufficient for traditional IAM capabilities. CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian is a robust AI IAM and security offering focused on endpoints and WebHook-based agent controls. Zscaler’s network-centric Agent Trust controls overlap and complement that functionality.
- **Expect more complete OT solutions as the vendors combine offerings.** CrowdStrike and Zscaler both have OT csolutions that, on their own, only cover small aspects for protecting critical infrastructure. Bringing solutions together creates an opportunity to produce offerings that can discover the operational assets, their business process role, the risk exposure of these devices, and provide layered controls to protect these assets from attacks or inadvertent exposure to unauthorized users and systems. The challenge will be ensuring that the combined company maintains its integrations. This is because the majority of OT/industrial control system environments are heterogeneous and expecting a “rip-and-replace” approach will have customers looking for vendors that can seamlessly integrate with existing infrastructure.
- **Complete workplace security with complementary capabilities** . Securing the core elements of the user workspace — desktop, mobile, and browser — has been a push for CrowdStrike with its existing EDR/XDR, the growing development of its mobile threat defense offering, and the Seraphic acquisition earlier this year. Zscaler includes its own browser security from its SquareX acquisition, which will require combining two separate approaches to browser security into one solid product. But this also means integrating Falcon Guardian into all aspects of the user endpoint to secure agentic workflows and agents on those endpoints, as well as seamlessly integrate with existing agents on these endpoint platforms.
- **Don’t write off standalone SASE.** Even with the push to one-stop platforms, standalone SASE won’t disappear. With more than 20 vendors claiming to offer SASE, the market remains immature, fragmented, and influenced by forces much larger than any single acquisition. This deal won’t reshape the SASE market overnight. CrowdStrike will likely try to maintain its multivendor positioning, even as Cato Networks, Netskope, Versa Networks, and others shift their partnerships. Enterprises should continue to balance integrated suites against specialized products based on architecture, operational models, existing investments, and integration. Security, infrastructure, and network teams must learn to work together as tools and teams become more tightly integrated. AI agents, autonomous operations, and other emerging technologies will intensify that pressure by requiring richer context and coordinated policy across endpoints, identities, applications, networks, and security controls.
